forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Peterborough forecasts £7.9m overspend on £258m budget, £7.7m of it in children's services
news_drafts.lead:
Peterborough City Council expects to spend £7.9m more than planned in 2026/27 on its day-to-day running costs (revenue spending: staff, services and contracts). That is 3.1% over a net budget of £258m, according to a first-quarter report to its cabinet on 1 October. Children and Young People accounts for £7.7m of the total.

The largest single line is placements for children in care, forecast to overspend by £5.2m. The budget assumed 429 children in care and 41 residential placements. The number of children in care was 444 in June, and residential placements stood at 47 in August. The average price of the last ten residential placements is £9,000 a week against £6,500 budgeted, and nine children are in placements costing more than £10,000 a week. Residential care makes up £3.2m of the £5.2m placement overspend.

If the overspend continues to the year end, the council will have to draw on its general fund reserves, the money set aside as a cushion for the unexpected. The report forecasts the balance falling from £10.5m at the start of the year to £6.7m by 31 March 2027, a 36% reduction. Total usable reserves, money the council can actually spend, are £23.7m, excluding the deficit on schools funding. Of that, £6.8m, or 29%, is ringfenced for specific purposes.

news_drafts.headline: Peterborough schools grant forecast to overspend by £16.6m in 2026/27, taking deficit to £17.7m
news_drafts.lead:
Peterborough City Council expects to overspend its dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) by £16.6m in 2026/27, according to the first-quarter budget monitoring report (the in-year check of spending against budget) presented to Cabinet on 1 October. That would leave a cumulative deficit of £17.7m by 31 March 2027.

The report attributes the overspend to increased demand for Education, Health and Care Plans, the legal documents that set out support for children with special educational needs and disabilities. This spending falls under high needs, the part of school funding for those children.

The Department for Education (DfE) has committed to fund 90% of deficits held at 31 March 2026. For deficits arising in 2026/27 and 2027/28, the paper quotes the government as saying: "local authorities can expect that we will continue to take an appropriate and proportionate approach, though it will not be unlimited." From 2028/29, the report says, spending on special educational needs and disabilities is to be covered within the government's departmental expenditure limit, its fixed spending budget for departments. The papers do not say how much of the new deficit the government will fund.

news_drafts.headline: Peterborough sets up Property Board after January statutory report on John Mansfield Centre sale
news_drafts.lead:
Peterborough City Council has created an internal Property Board to scrutinise property decisions before they are taken, after its chief finance officer issued a statutory report in January 2026 on the disposal of the John Mansfield Centre. The council's Annual Governance Statement action plan, before the Audit Committee on 23 September, says oversight of decision notices on property transactions "required improvement".

The report was issued under sections 5 and 114 of the relevant legislation. A section 114 notice is a formal warning from the chief finance officer that the council cannot balance its budget, which freezes new spending until councillors agree a plan. Cabinet has since retrospectively approved four historic decisions on commercial leases that exceeded the £250,000 aggregate rental threshold.

The plan also covers procurement. An external review of the procurement function made 49 recommendations, and the council is tracking which are underway, which it regards as unattainable and which still need progressing. Temporary accommodation procurement has concluded, with 11 suppliers awarded contracts, and the council describes it as now compliant. Cabinet agreed longer-term arrangements on 23 March 2026. The council's own paper says procurement and contract management "remain areas of elevated risk".
news_drafts.paper_title: Appendix B: Annual Governance Statement Action Plan

findings.headline: The council is the subject of a paused Local Government Reorganisation and will remain responsible for local services for at least one additional MTFS year.
findings.detail: The paper states that the government's decision to pause LGR has materially altered the council's position, reducing the immediate need to prepare for implementation but creating uncertainty over future timescales. The council will remain responsible for local services for at least one additional MTFS year.
findings.matters: A finance director elsewhere in a two-tier or reorganising area would want to know how the pause changes the timetable for stable baselines and transition funding.
findings.quote: It also means the Council will remain responsible for local services for at least one additional MTFS year.

findings.headline: The employer pension contribution rate is reduced to 14.4% from 1 April 2026, following a projected Cambridgeshire Pension Fund surplus of £271m.
findings.detail: The 2025 actuarial valuation identified a projected surplus of £271m, £116m higher than at the previous valuation. Following actuarial advice, the council's employer contribution rate was reduced to 14.4% from 1 April 2026, with no cash lump-sum payment, and confirmed for 2026/27 to 2028/29.
findings.matters: A lower employer contribution rate for three years reduces a major cost line, and the rate for 2029/30 is not yet known, which affects planning for other councils in the same fund.
findings.figures: 14.4% employer contribution rate; £271m projected surplus; £116m higher than previous valuation
findings.quote: with no cash lump-sum payment. This rate was confirmed for each of the three years from 2026/27 to 2028/29.

findings.headline: Recovery Grant of £6,025k a year to 2028/29 could be withdrawn after the current settlement, with the council assuming £2,944k in 2029/30
findings.detail: The paper states the Recovery Grant is targeted at councils with high deprivation-related needs and limited Council Tax-raising capacity. It says that if the grant is withdrawn when the current multi-year settlement ends, the council could face a greater reduction in funding from 2029/30 than currently assumed.
findings.matters: A large one-off-style grant that may not continue beyond the settlement is a funding risk that other councils with similar deprivation profiles would be assessing.
findings.figures: £6,025k Recovery Grant in 2026/27 to 2028/29; £2,944k in 2029/30; total funding £257,749k in 2026/27 rising to £322,613k in 2029/30
findings.quote: If it is withdrawn when the current multi-year settlement ends, the Council could face a greater reduction in funding from 2029/30 than currently assumed.

findings.headline: Clare Lodge income is materially below budget because occupancy is much lower than anticipated.
findings.detail: The paper says Clare Lodge continues to generate a positive financial contribution overall, but income remains materially below budget. It attributes the reduction in occupancy to Ofsted restrictions and regulatory scrutiny in 2025/26. The council has proposed increasing planned reserve contributions for the service by £1m in each of the three years of the MTFS.
findings.matters: A specialist secure children's unit with lower occupancy after regulatory restrictions is a concentration of income risk that a lender or a finance director at another council running a similar unit would weigh.
findings.figures: £1m increase in planned reserve contributions in each of the three years
findings.quote: due to much lower than anticipated and budgeted occupancy levels.

findings.headline: Recent children's residential placements average over £9k per week (£470k annually), up from nearly £7k per week (£347k) in February 2026
findings.detail: The paper says the average cost of recent placements made by the council is over £9k per week (£470k annually), up from just under £7k per week (£347k annually) in February 2026. The highest recent placement is just under £17k per week. The number of children in care is rising from 436 in March 2025 to a forecast 466 by March 2027.
findings.matters: Rising unit costs in residential placements, not only numbers, drive the budget, and the same market dynamic applies to any council buying residential care for children.
findings.figures: over £9k per week (£470k annually) for recent placements; just under £7k per week (£347k annually) in February 2026; just under £17k per week (£886k annually) highest; 436 children in March 2025; 466 forecast by March 2027
findings.quote: the average cost of recent placements made by the Council has been over £9k per week (£470k annually).

daily_post.headline: Stanground Bypass Adoption Improvements: council to fund £3.189m scheme through prudential borrowing, preserving reserves, at c£400k annual cost over 12-year life
daily_post.lead: Reverses normal councils' preference to minimise debt and use reserves. Signals that maintaining liquid reserves is now more critical priority than minimising borrowing. Decision acknowledges financial stress and need to preserve cash flexibility.…
